Schedule estimates after accounting for absences

Measured absences change the schedule estimates little. Adding absence value to the regression moves every schedule coefficient by under 9%. Unmeasured absences and changes in minutes can still matter.

Show coefficient comparison
Limits of the comparison

Availability is measured after the game. Every figure here is worked out after the fact, from who actually took the floor. Lineups are not settled until shortly before tip, so none of this forecasts a game.

Much of the margin remains unexplained. Final margins have a standard deviation of 13.9 points; the model's error after including team records, schedule, and absences is 12.6 points.

Absence is inferred from the rotation a team had actually been using, because a long-term injury can keep a player off the sheet entirely. A player who misses four straight games leaves that rotation, so a long absence counts for its first four games only. Each team can be measured from its sixth regular-season game, once the rotation comes from that season's regular-season games. Both teams need usable histories for a game to enter the margin comparison, which covers 1997-98 through 2025-26 after source checks.

LATE-GAME AND HOME-AWAY COMPARISONS

Late-game variation does not exceed the chance expectation. Across 12,403 games, the league calls 0.92 fouls in the last 2 minutes of a fourth quarter, 8.5% of that quarter’s fouls. The number of officials crossing the comparison threshold is 2 against 3.4 expected by chance. This test compares officials; it cannot determine whether officials collectively pass up calls or whether any individual call was correct.

Home-away foul counts differ modestly. Home teams are called for 0.19 fewer shooting fouls a game than visitors, and officials do differ in how far they lean that way: splitting each one’s home-minus-away gap by foul type puts 7 of them past the bar on shooting fouls and 7 on personals, against the 3.4 that noise alone produces among 74 officials. These counts exceed the chance expectation, but the home-away spread is about one foul per game across officials. Crew assignment and team behaviour limit what can be attributed to an individual.

THE FEATURED PLAYOFF RECORD

Opponents faced with Foster had a slightly lower mean regular-season win rate than those faced without him: 0.599 against 0.606 by win rate. Of the 689 official-and-player pairs with at least 10 shared playoff games, this one ranks #1 in this dataset.

Chance also produces extreme records. Across 689 pairs, a rough reference for the minimum p-value is 0.00145. Scott Foster and Chris Paul come in at p = 0.0016, less extreme than that reference. This 1/N reference approximates the expected minimum for independent tests with uniformly distributed null p-values. These pairs share games and players, so it is not a calibrated minimum-p distribution or an adjusted significance threshold.

In the full grid, 7 pairs clear p < 0.01 compared with a simple N × 0.01 reference of 6.9, and 27 clear p < 0.05 compared with an N × 0.05 reference of 34.5. These descriptive comparisons alone do not establish an excess of extreme pairs.

GAMES AFTER THE CLAIM BECAME KNOWN

A claim found by looking can only be confirmed on games nobody had seen when they found it. This one was in circulation by the end of 2019-20. Before then, Chris Paul was 0–6 with Scott Foster, and after it was famous, 1–4.

Both periods are too small for the declared test. Both halves fall under the 10 shared games this page requires before it will evaluate a pair. That threshold was written down before the analysis. The available later games therefore cannot provide the planned confirmation test.

WHILE WE ARE HERE · MAKE-UP CALLS

Consecutive calls switch teams more often than after shuffling. Across 498,007 consecutive foul pairs, the next whistle goes against the other team 52.4% of the time, against 50.5% when you shuffle the same game’s calls into a random order, with t = 27.4.

Shuffling also removes possession order. After an offensive foul, the fouling team turns the ball over and defends. If possession drives the pattern, the next foul may be on that same team; a simple make-up-call explanation predicts a switch.

STAR FOUL TROUBLE

Two first-quarter fouls are associated with fewer minutes. They occur in 6.2% of 21,400 star-games, with 1.17 fewer minutes than the player's own average. Across 73 officials the spread is 1.01× what random assignment produces, at p = 0.4535. The rates are 6.2% on the road against 6.1% at home, a gap of 0.09 percentage points.

HOW TO READ ANY OF THIS

Three officials work every game and the play-by-play never records which one made a call, so every figure on this page credits all three and cannot isolate an individual effect. None of it separates a correct call from an incorrect one. The questions, the thresholds and the five named claims were all fixed in writing before the playoff data was fetched (ml/referee_player_preregistration.md). Results are published even when they do not meet their declared evidence thresholds.

WHAT THESE NUMBERS CANNOT DO

Every game credits all three officials because the play-by-play does not identify who made each call. Changing crewmates may reduce the influence of any one partner, but the analysis cannot isolate an individual official's contribution.

None of this is a fairness claim. Calling more offensive fouls says nothing about whom an official favors, and no measurement on this page distinguishes a correct call from an incorrect one. It measures how often each kind of call is recorded.

The problem

“They looked tired” is easy to say after a loss. Checking that idea requires schedules, results and a fair comparison group.

FullCourt brings those records together so a fan can inspect the conditions and see how much the historical pattern actually supports.

SCOPE

Three implementation decisions
01
Calculate schedule load before a visitor opens a page
PROBLEM
A single game depends on both teams’ recent games, travel and rest. Repeating that work for every visitor would tie page delivery to historical calculations.
BUILT
The pipeline computes fatigue scores on the write path. Game pages read stored scores and attach the schedule facts needed to explain them.
TRADEOFF
Reads stay simpler. A change to the calculation requires a deliberate data rebuild, and missing stored scores must remain visibly unavailable.
Read the fatigue engine
src/lib/fatigue.ts ↗
02
Choose delivery around how the data changes
PROBLEM
A game slate, a historical player table and an NBA report do not need the same loading strategy.
BUILT
Database-backed views serve games and season comparisons. Shooting and other research views use generated artifacts. Officiating fetches each report’s detail when it is opened.
TRADEOFF
Published research remains reproducible, with smaller initial report payloads. Refreshing it requires validation and deployment rather than an invisible live replacement.
Read report loading
src/components/officiating-report.tsx ↗
03
Make the evidence travel with the link
PROBLEM
A shared finding is hard to inspect if its season, filters and selected game disappear when someone opens it.
BUILT
Selected views use URL state. Reports retain NBA source links and verdict text. Method articles preserve section anchors and open linked evidence.
TRADEOFF
URLs require validation and reliable browser-history behavior. The payoff is a view that another person can inspect and revisit.
Read sharing and recovery tests
e2e/officiating.spec.ts ↗
04
What gets checked
Calculations and artifacts

Unit and Python contract tests check calculations and published artifacts.

Browser behavior

Browser tests exercise filters, keyboard behavior, deep links and failure recovery. The suite runs separately against a populated environment.

Every change

CI runs lint, types, tests, the production build and a dependency audit.

NOT ENOUGH ALONE
Passing automated tests is only part of verification: visible claims still need to match the source records.

Verification workflow ↗
05
A lesson from reviewing the product

A usability review found three problems.

A schedule-density approximation
It was presented as an exact game count. The label now distinguishes the underlying facts.
Altitude carryover
The code charged it at any gap after a visit to altitude, where the methodology said the next night. It measured no effect, so it was removed.
Mobile month controls
The controls worked, but the selected month was outside the visible area.

A passing calculation test or accessibility scan cannot establish that a sentence is accurate or a control is easy to use. Check the complete path from record to interpretation.

06
What remains uncertain
Historical comparisons
They include differences in team strength, venue and other conditions.
Player rest splits
They can be noisy.
NBA officiating reports
They cover selected late-game situations.

FullCourt keeps those limits beside the findings and preserves tests that did not support a clear effect.

BEHIND THE DATA · REST ADVANTAGE
Rest advantage

How the fatigue score is built, term by term, and how its results compare with home court.

Keep in mind
Rested and tired teams also differ in home court and team strength. These win rates do not isolate rest, and they do not predict a single game.

On this page
How the score works

Each team gets a fatigue score from its schedule before tip-off. A higher score means a more tired team. The rest advantage is the gap between the two teams’ scores.

load  = workload + travel + road

score = load × backToBack
             × altitude × density
        + freshness + overtime

edge  = awayScore − homeScore

The three loads are added together. Back-to-back, altitude and density multiply that total. Freshness and overtime are added last, and a score never goes below 0. A positive edge means the home team is fresher.

A gap under 0.5 counts as no edge. That covers 8,307 games (17.6% of this sample), which make no rest claim either way.

BEHIND THE DATA · SCHEDULE EDGE
Schedule edge

How each team's schedule is scored for and against it within one season, and what that is worth in wins.

Keep in mind
Worth prices the schedule with historical rates. It is not the number of wins a team actually gained.

On this page
Counting favorable and unfavorable games

Every game has a rest advantage: the gap between the two teams’ fatigue scores. A game is favorable when the opponent is more tired by at least 0.5, and unfavorable when the team is. The season total is one minus the other.

net = favorable − unfavorable

favorable    gap ≥ 0.5, team fresher
unfavorable  gap ≥ 0.5, team tired
3+ edge      gap ≥ 3, either side

Played and projected games both count. A game is left out when either team has no earlier game that season, because its fatigue score has nothing to build on. A missing score is not treated as an even game.

Every game is counted once from each side, so the league’s net totals add up to zero. That is a check on the arithmetic, not a finding.

BEHIND THE DATA · PLAYER SHOOTING BY REST
Player Shooting by Rest

Player shooting on no rest compared with two to 29 days off, with shot counts and uncertainty for each split.

Keep in mind
A positive split means better shooting with more rest. Opponents, shot choice and why games were missed can also move it.

On this page
The two rest groups

Rest is counted from the player’s own games, not the team’s. A player back after a week away is rested even if the team played last night.

no rest     played the day before
rested      2 to 29 full days off

rest effect = eFG% rested
            − eFG% no rest

The table labels the rested group “2+ days rest”; its exact range is two to 29 full days off (three to 30 days since the previous appearance). An appearance counts even with no shot attempt. NBA Cup games count toward rest; the shooting numbers use regular-season shots only.

Left out: games after exactly one day off, and games after 30 or more days off, including season openers and returns from long absences. This is a long-absence filter based on the gap between appearances, not an injury flag. Shorter injury absences can remain in the rested group. Orlando bubble shots are left out too, though bubble games still count toward rest.

Shooting efficiency: eFG%

Shooting is measured as effective field goal percentage (eFG%). It counts a made three as 1.5 made twos, for the extra point.

eFG% = 100 × (FGM + 0.5 × 3PM)
             ÷ FGA

Playoff Rest

A separate model for playoff series, built on team records and prior-round workload, and scored on probability quality and winner accuracy.

On this page
What the model predicts

For each playoff series, the model gives the probability that the home-court team wins it. That team comes from the series schedule, so it is not always the higher seed.

p = P(home-court team wins series)

p ≥ 0.5  →  pick the home-court team
p < 0.5  →  pick the opponent

This model has its own inputs and weights. It does not use the regular-season fatigue score, and playoff games are left out of the regular-season win rates. Played playoff games still count toward workload.

BEHIND THE DATA · AVAILABILITY COST
Availability cost

How missing rotation players relate to final margin. Absences are known only after a game is played, so nothing here forecasts tonight's lineup.

Keep in mind
Absences are known only after a game. Nothing here says who plays tonight, and the separate absence effects must not be added together.

On this page
Who counts as a missing player

A missing player is someone in the team’s recent rotation who did not play. The rotation comes from earlier games, because a box score can leave out players who sat.

rotation  2+ appearances with minutes
          in the team's last 5 games
          this season, averaging
          15+ minutes

missing   in the rotation, but did
          not play tonight
ROTATION WINDOW
5 games
earlier games this season
ROTATION THRESHOLD
15 min
average per appearance
TYPICAL ROTATION
8.7
players, measured

A long absence counts for at most its first four games. After four straight misses, the player no longer has 2 games in the window. A player with fewer recent games can drop out sooner.

The window restarts each season, so a team is measured from its sixth game, and players who left in the off-season never count as missing. The short window follows trades, coaching choices and injuries. It can miss a player whose minutes were already falling before an injury.

A confirmed appearance counts as present even when its minutes are unclear. Games where unclear participation could change the result are left out, which thins older seasons most. An unclear box score is never read as proof of an absence.

BEHIND THE DATA · SHOT VALUE
Expected Shot Value

A model estimate of shot value at each court location, fitted to league shooting data. Defender position and shooter skill are outside this model.

Keep in mind
Every shot from the same cell in the same season gets the same value, whoever shot it and however it was guarded.

On this page
Expected value by court location

The half court is split into one-foot cells. For each cell, the model estimates how often a two and a three go in, then blends them by how often the league shoots each from that cell in that season.

r3    = threes ÷ all shots in the cell

xeFG% = 100 × [ (1 − r3) × P(two)
              + r3 × 1.5 × P(three) ]

P(two) and P(three) are make probabilities. The 1.5 is the eFG% credit for the extra point on a three.

xeFG% is the model’s estimate for league-average shooting at a spot. The difference view shows the location model minus the zone baseline, in percentage points. It compares two models, not a team’s shooting with an expectation.

A three can go in less often than a two and still be worth more. The eFG% scale accounts for the extra point.

BEHIND THE DATA · OFFICIATING
Officiating

How we count errors in the NBA's Last Two Minute reports.

Keep in mind
These are the NBA's own reviews of selected close-game endings. They cannot measure whole-game accuracy or say which official erred.

On this page
Which games are reviewed

Since 2017–18, the NBA publishes a report for every game within three points at any time in the last two minutes of the fourth quarter or overtime. Each report grades the calls, and the important non-calls, in that stretch. FullCourt shows regular-season reports only.

Reports began on March 2, 2015, so 2014–15 is a partial season. Before 2017–18, a game qualified if it was within five points at the two-minute mark. The NBA has also changed how it presents calls over time, which limits comparisons across eras.

We check that every report in the NBA's archive or season index was collected. We do not check whether that index lists every eligible game.

NBA report criteria and definitions ↗

What the verdicts mean
CODE	NBA VERDICT	MEANING
INC	Incorrect non-call	A missed call; counted as an error.
IC	Incorrect call	An incorrect whistle; counted as an error.
CC	Correct call	A correct whistle; retained in the report.
CNC	Correct non-call	Correctly allowing play to continue; retained in the report.
missed-call share = missed calls
                    ÷ all errors

errors per game   = all errors
                    ÷ reviewed games

An error is an INC or an IC. Ungraded entries stay visible and are not counted as correct. Old labels “Undetectable”, “NCI” and “NCC” are kept separately and left out of error counts; we do not guess what NCI or NCC meant.

Time zones

Does playing far east of home on short rest help explain results? A pre-registered test found it did not improve held-out predictions.

The question tested

The fatigue model already includes time-zone shifts. The weight-fitting work in ADR 0006 tested them as a general effect and found they added no predictive value. This test asks something narrower.

The question: does a visitor do worse at a venue at least 3 clock hours east of its home base, on short rest (it played the night before)? The shift compares home base with tonight’s arena, not with the last game’s, so it says nothing about the actual flight.

16
